title: Magnetic Particle Inspection for LNG | MPI, US Terminals
description: On-site magnetic particle inspection for US LNG plants: carbon steel, tank attachments and 9% nickel steel with demagnetization planned. Request a quote.
h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection for LNG Facilities in the United States
html:
Magnetic particle inspection (MPI) at an LNG facility has a narrow but real job: finding surface and near-surface cracks in ferromagnetic carbon steel and 9% nickel steel welds, supports and repairs. It does not work on austenitic stainless steel or aluminum, which is most of the cold piping. Atlantis mobilizes qualified technicians anywhere in the United States for that scope; request an MT inspection quote and we will tell you which components belong to MT and which belong to penetrant.

Why MT is a limited tool in an LNG plant

Magnetic particle testing relies on a magnetic field that leaks out of the surface wherever a crack interrupts it. The part therefore has to be ferromagnetic. In an LNG terminal that excludes the 304L and 316L stainless steel used for cryogenic process piping, the aluminum in brazed plate-fin and spiral-wound exchangers, and the weld metal of any joint made with austenitic filler. It includes the carbon steel structure around them and the 9% nickel steel used for inner tanks.

That is why a competent LNG inspection plan uses MT selectively. A buyer who asks for 100% MT on stainless piping has asked for something no technician can deliver, and a good vendor says so before mobilizing. The sibling pages explain what covers the gaps: liquid penetrant testing for LNG for nonmagnetic metals and ultrasonic testing for LNG for internal flaws and wall thickness.

Components where MT is the right choice

  • Storage tank outer shells, roofs and bottoms in carbon steel: welded seams, nozzle reinforcement welds, and attachment welds for platforms, stairs and piping supports.
  • Pipe supports, racks and structural steel: fillet welds on shoes, guides, anchors and saddles on the warm and cold pipe racks, checked to the owner's structural specification and AWS D1.1 where the project invokes it.
  • Pressure vessel and piping repairs in carbon steel: weld repair excavations, final weld surfaces, and temporary attachment removal areas, per ASME Section VIII or B31.3 as applicable.
  • Lifting equipment and crane components: hooks, lugs, pad eyes and spreader beams used for module and equipment lifts at terminals and fabrication yards.
  • 9% nickel steel tank welds and repairs: a selective use, discussed below, because the material is magnetic but carries its own handling rules.

The 9% nickel steel question: residual magnetism and arc blow

Nine percent nickel steel is ferromagnetic, so MT can be used on it. The catch is what the magnetic field leaves behind. Magnetizing a heavy 9% nickel plate, particularly with a direct-current method or a lot of repeated passes, can leave residual magnetism in the steel. That residual field deflects the welding arc, a defect called arc blow, and makes later welding, repair or tie-in work harder to control and more likely to produce lack of fusion.

Atlantis therefore plans demagnetization and field control with the owner before any MT is done on cryogenic nickel steel. In practice that means choosing an alternating-current yoke technique where the specification allows, avoiding prod contact that can leave arc burns on cold-service steel, measuring the residual field with a gauss meter when the owner's welding specification sets a limit, and demagnetizing the area when it is needed. The acceptance limit comes from the owner's specification, not from us. Where a customer prefers to avoid magnetizing the nickel steel at all, penetrant testing of the finished weld surface is the usual alternative.

Codes and acceptance for LNG MT

The legal framework is the same as for every method at a US LNG site: PHMSA 49 CFR Part 193 with NFPA 59A for onshore facilities, FERC authorization for terminals, and the construction codes for each item. API 620 and API 625 cover tanks, and ASME B31.3 covers process piping. The examination method follows ASME Section V Article 7, and ASTM E709 is commonly cited for the practice. Acceptance criteria come from the construction code or the owner's specification, typically as limits on linear indications and rounded indications. The owner's inspector decides acceptance; we report what the examination shows.

How the examination is performed

The technician starts with a surface that has been cleaned of paint, scale, oil and weld spatter to a level the procedure sets. On carbon steel structure, a typical field technique uses an electromagnetic yoke with the legs placed across the weld in two directions roughly perpendicular to each other, so cracks in any orientation interrupt the field. Lifting force is checked against the procedure's requirement before use, and the field is verified with a pie gauge or a similar indicator on the part.

Visible dry or wet particles are used in good light, and fluorescent wet particles are used in darker, shaded areas with a black light and a darkened work zone. Indications are evaluated, marked and sketched. If something is relevant, the technician measures its length and location, and where the specification allows, the area is lightly dressed and re-examined. After testing, parts are demagnetized where the procedure requires and cleaned of residual particles so they do not interfere with coating or later non-destructive testing.

Temperature, surface and access limits

MT is sensitive to the surface. Heavy coatings reduce sensitivity above the thickness the procedure allows; thicker paint is removed locally or the procedure is qualified on a coated block. Hot surfaces degrade particle suspension and dry particles can burn, so high-temperature lines are examined only within the procedure's range. Cold surfaces carry frost and condensation; wet methods need the surface dry and above the dew point, and the technician works at the insulation windows the owner opens. Rough weld profiles, undercut and spatter can hide or mimic indications and are called out in the report.

Flaws MT is looking for in LNG work

The damage mechanisms differ from a refinery. Clean cryogenic service rarely corrodes metal, so the flaws of interest are fabrication and thermal-cycle related: hydrogen-assisted cold cracking near welds in thicker carbon steel sections, lack of fusion at weld toes, crater cracks at weld stops, arc strikes left by fit-up and temporary attachments, and fatigue cracks starting at the toes of support welds where piping movement and thermal contraction load the joint. Tie-in welds between prefabricated modules and the main structure are a common place for these, because they are made in the field under restraint.

Lifting and rigging points are worth separate mention. Modular liquefaction construction depends on heavy lifts, and a crack in a lug or pad eye is a safety issue before it is a code issue. MT of lifting attachments before and after a lift campaign is routine, and the report states the load rating marking and the component ID so the lift file is complete. Attachment welds removed after fit-up are ground flush and checked, since a gouge or crack left in a pressure-containing wall is the kind of defect that surfaces later under thermal cycling.

Choosing between MT and PT on a mixed-metal joint

A single LNG joint can combine metals. A carbon steel support welded to a stainless pipe, or a nickel steel nozzle welded to a carbon steel shell, puts a nonmagnetic weld zone beside a magnetic base metal. MT on such a joint finds cracks in the magnetic side and may miss them in the nonmagnetic filler, so the procedure states which zones MT covers and the plan adds penetrant testing for the rest. That decision is easiest to make from the weld map before mobilization, which is one reason we ask for it in the quote request.

What to send for an MT quote

  • Drawings or weld maps showing the joints, and the material for each
  • Whether any of the steel is 9% nickel, and the owner's residual magnetism limit if there is one
  • Applicable code, specification and acceptance criteria
  • Coating and insulation status, and who prepares the surfaces
  • Access method, permits, and any hot-work or confined-space rules
  • Site address, TWIC requirements, and the site contact

Planning for US LNG sites

Sites are secured under Coast Guard and FERC conditions, and work usually needs a permit and gas monitoring. Wet fluorescent testing needs a dark zone, which can be hard to achieve outdoors in daylight, so the work is staged under a tent or at night where the site allows. Ignition-source controls matter for yokes and any equipment near classified areas. Technicians travel to your site for the agreed scope, and the owner arranges access, power and the orientation required for the crew.

Where we work in the US for LNG

  • Corpus Christi: coastal liquefaction trains and pipe racks with extensive carbon steel structure and supports.
  • Lake Charles: Calcasieu Channel facilities, where large vessel and tank repair work calls for MT on welded attachments.
  • Beaumont: Sabine-Neches area plants and fabricators close to the export terminals.
  • Houston: fabrication shops where LNG modules, skids and lifting equipment are built and tested.
  • Savannah: Georgia coast terminals and port-side lifting equipment.
  • Baltimore: Chesapeake region facilities and marine structures serving the Maryland export site.

Training your own MT technicians

Terminal operators and fabricators building in-house capability can study with MT Level 1 training and MT Level 2 training, and rehearse on the magnetic particle simulator. The employer certifies under its written practice; see written practice development for setting that up. The national guides are magnetic particle testing services and the MT versus PT comparison.

What we do not do here

Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States, does not run in-line inspection tools and does not offer specialist techniques outside MT, PT and UT. We do not perform MT on austenitic stainless steel because it cannot work, and we will not quote it. We also do not calculate remaining life or approve repair decisions, which belong to the owner's engineer.

faq.q: Can magnetic particle testing be used on stainless steel LNG piping?
faq.a: Not on austenitic grades such as 304L and 316L, because they are not ferromagnetic and cannot hold the field MT needs. Penetrant testing is the surface method for those welds, and ultrasonic testing covers internal flaws.

faq.q: Is 9% nickel steel safe to examine with MT?
faq.a: Yes, 9% nickel steel is ferromagnetic and can be examined. The risk is residual magnetism and arc blow during later welding, so demagnetization and field limits are planned with the owner before work starts.

faq.q: Why do you prefer yokes to prods on cryogenic steel?
faq.a: Prod contact can leave arc burns, which are a defect on cold-service steel. An alternating-current yoke also leaves less residual field than many direct-current methods, though the procedure and owner specification make the final call.

faq.q: What codes do you use for MT at LNG sites?
faq.a: The method follows ASME Section V Article 7, with ASTM E709 as common practice. Acceptance criteria come from API 620, API 625, ASME B31.3 or the owner specification under PHMSA 49 CFR Part 193 and NFPA 59A.

faq.q: Can you do MT through coatings?
faq.a: Thin, well-adhered coatings can be tolerated if the procedure was qualified for them, but heavy or damaged coatings reduce sensitivity. We confirm the coating thickness limit in the quote and remove paint locally where needed.

When the procedure or specification requires it, yes. We also demagnetize and measure the field where later welding, machining or instrument installation could be affected, and we record the method in the report.

faq.q: Who accepts or rejects MT indications?
faq.a: Our Level II technician evaluates and records indications against the named criteria, and the owner's inspector or engineer accepts, rejects or orders repair. An ASNT Level III approves our procedure and reviews the report.

faq.q: What do you need from us for an MT quote?
faq.a: Drawings or weld maps, material for each joint including any 9% nickel steel, the code and acceptance criteria, coating and insulation status, access, permits and the site address with TWIC requirements.

faq.q: Is MT or PT better on LNG carbon steel attachment welds?
faq.a: MT is usually faster and finds near-surface cracks that penetrant can miss under paint residue or smearing, so it is favored on carbon steel. PT remains the choice where the steel is nonmagnetic or the owner wants no magnetization.
